header_title: Energy Is a Strange Kind of Counting
tagline: The most important law is a bookkeeping rule
audio_script: There is a fact, or if you wish a law, governing all natural phenomena that are known to date. There is no known exception. The law is called the conservation of energy. It says that there is a certain quantity, which we call energy, that does not change in the manifold changes which nature undergoes. That is a most abstract idea because it is a mathematical principle. It is not a description of a mechanism. It is just a strange fact that we can calculate some number and when we finish watching nature go through her tricks and calculate the number again, it is the same. We have no knowledge of what energy is. We do not have a picture that energy comes in little blobs of a definite amount. It is an abstract thing in that it does not tell us the mechanism or the reasons for the various formulas.

header_title: How Far Does a Drunken Sailor Get?
audio_script: Imagine a drunken sailor comes out of a bar and takes a sequence of steps. Each step is chosen at an arbitrary angle at random. The question is, after a long time, where is he? Of course we do not know. It is impossible to say. But on the average, how far away from the bar has he gone? The answer is beautiful. The mean square of the distance from the origin is proportional to the number of steps. Not the distance itself. The square of the distance. This is the characteristic of a random walk. If the sailor were drifting at a nice uniform velocity, the mean distance would be proportional to time. It is not. Only the mean square distance grows with time. So he does make headway, but only as the square root of the number of steps. That is why a tiny particle jiggling in water, bombarded by molecules, spreads out slowly. It is the same mathematics.

tagline: One law explains planets and apples
audio_script: In this chapter we discuss one of the most far-reaching generalizations of the human mind. The law of gravitation: every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force which is proportional to the mass of each and varies inversely as the square of the distance between them. That is the whole law. If to this we add the fact that an object responds to a force by accelerating in the direction of the force by an amount inversely proportional to the mass, we shall have said everything required. Newton used the second and third of Kepler's laws to deduce this. Then he predicted. His analysis of the moon's motion connected the falling of objects on the earth's surface with that of the moon. It turned out beautifully. Wishing to put this theory to a test, Newton made his calculations very carefully and found a discrepancy so large that he regarded the theory as contradicted. Six years later a new measurement of the size of the earth showed that the astronomers had been using an incorrect distance to the moon. When Newton heard of this, he made the calculation again, and obtained beautiful agreement.

header_title: What Does Sixty Miles an Hour Really Mean?
tagline: Speed is a limit of a ratio
audio_script: Many physicists think that measurement is the only definition of anything. So we should use the instrument that measures speed, the speedometer, and say: your speedometer reads sixty. But she can say the speedometer is broken. Does that mean the car is standing still? We believe there is something to measure before we build the speedometer. Let us see if we can get a better definition of the idea. If the lady kept on going for another one-thousandth of an hour, she would go one-thousandth of sixty miles. The point is that for a moment she is going at that speed. What that means is that if she went just a little bit more in time, the extra distance she goes would be the same as that of a car that goes at a steady sixty. So we ask: how far do we go in a very short time? We divide that distance by the time, and that gives the speed. But the time should be made as short as possible. The shorter, the better. That is a successful answer. It is the definition that we are going to use. This idea was invented by Newton and by Leibniz, independently, and is the beginning of a new branch of mathematics: the differential calculus.

tagline: Every push has a matching push-back
audio_script: Newton gave one rule about the force: that the forces between interacting bodies are equal and opposite. Action equals reaction. What is meant is something of this kind. Suppose we have two small bodies, and the first exerts a force on the second, pushing it with a certain force. Then, simultaneously, according to Newton's third law, the second particle will push on the first with an equal force, in the opposite direction. Furthermore, these forces effectively act in the same line. For the moment we shall take it to be true that action equals reaction. If there is a third particle, not on the same line as the other two, the law does not mean that the total force on the first one is equal to the total force on the second. The result is that the total effect on the first two is in some other direction. However, the forces on each particle can be resolved into parts, and each pair of particles has corresponding components of mutual interaction that are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. What is the interesting consequence? If the rate of change of momentum of one particle is always equal and opposite to that of another, then the total momentum does not change. That is the law of conservation of momentum.

header_title: Why Vectors Are So Useful in Physics
tagline: They carry the symmetry of the laws
audio_script: Why do we want to use vectors in physics? The answer is that the laws of physics are symmetric under rotation of the coordinate system. If we write a physical relationship as a vector equation, then we are assured that the relationship is unchanged by a mere rotation of the coordinate axes. That is the reason vectors are so useful. Let us examine the laws of mechanics. We have three equations for each particle, one for each direction. But we can write them as one equation, mass times acceleration equals force, using vectors. The fact that a physical law can be written as a vector equation means that it does not depend on which way we choose the axes. That is a very powerful thing. It means we do not have to keep track of three equations. It means the structure of the law is a statement about the world, not about our arbitrary choice of coordinates. The very fact that we can say the same object is being described no matter how we turn the axes implies a physical intuition about the reality of a step in space that is independent of the components we measure it in.

header_title: One Equation Runs Half of Physics
audio_script: In the study of physics, a strange thing occurs again and again. The equations which appear in different fields of physics, and even in other sciences, are often almost exactly the same. The harmonic oscillator is one of these. We start with a mechanical example of a weight on a spring. But this equation appears again and again. The oscillations of a mass on a spring, the oscillations of charge flowing back and forth in an electrical circuit, the vibrations of a tuning fork, the analogous vibrations of the electrons in an atom which generate light waves, the equations for the operation of a servosystem, complicated interactions in chemical reactions, the growth of a colony of bacteria, foxes eating rabbits eating grass. All these follow equations which are very similar to one another. The equation is m times the second derivative of x equals minus k times x. The solution is a cosine. It has a period that depends only on the ratio of k to m. If we have a heavier mass it takes longer to oscillate. If the spring is stiffer it moves more quickly. But here is the beautiful thing: the period does not depend in any way on how the motion was started. The period is determined by the system. Only the amplitude is set by the initial conditions.

tagline: Three laws that unlocked the heavens
audio_script: First of all, Kepler found that each planet goes around the sun in a curve called an ellipse, with the sun at a focus of the ellipse. An ellipse is not just an oval but is a very specific and precise curve. Kepler's second observation was that the planets do not go around the sun at a uniform speed but move faster when they are nearer the sun and more slowly when they are farther from the sun. Suppose a planet is observed at any two successive times, say a week apart, and the radius vector is drawn to the planet for each observed position. The orbital arc traversed by the planet during the week, and the two radius vectors, bound a certain plane area. If two similar observations are made a week apart at a part of the orbit farther from the sun, the similarly bounded area is exactly the same as in the first case. The orbital speed is such that the radius sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Finally, a third law: the periods are proportional to the three-halves power of the orbit size. These three laws, discovered from Tycho Brahe's data, gave Newton the clue he needed to find the universal law of gravitation.

header_title: One Sentence Contains All of Chemistry
audio_script: If, in some cataclysm, all of scientific knowledge were to be destroyed, and only one sentence passed on to the next generations of creatures, what statement would contain the most information in the fewest words? I believe it is the atomic hypothesis that all things are made of atoms. Little particles that move around in perpetual motion, attracting each other when they are a little distance apart, but repelling upon being squeezed into one another. In that one sentence you will see there is an enormous amount of information about the world, if just a little imagination and thinking are applied. The atoms are one or two times ten to the minus eight centimeters in radius. Now ten to the minus eight centimeters is called an angstrom. Another way to remember their size is this. If an apple is magnified to the size of the earth, then the atoms in the apple are approximately the size of the original apple. Everything is made of atoms. That is the key hypothesis. The most important hypothesis in all of biology, for example, is that everything that animals do, atoms do. In other words, there is nothing that living things do that cannot be understood from the point of view that they are made of atoms acting according to the laws of physics.

header_title: Momentum Is Conserved Piece by Piece
tagline: We build up the law from experiments

audio_script: Now we would like to understand the law of conservation of momentum by means of experiments. Consider a track. Place three equally massive objects on it. Two are initially joined together with an explosive cylinder. The third is near but slightly separated, provided with a sticky bumper so it will stick to another object which hits it. A moment after the explosion we have two objects of mass m moving with equal and opposite velocities v. A moment after that, one of these collides with the third object and makes an object of mass 2m moving, so we believe, with velocity v over 2. How do we test whether it is really v over 2? By arranging the initial positions of the masses on the trough so that the distances to the ends are not equal, but are in the ratio two to one. Thus the first mass, which continues to move with velocity v, should cover twice as much distance in a given time as the two which are stuck together. The mass m and the mass 2m should reach the ends at the same time. And when we try it, we find they do. Now the next question. What will happen if a mass m with velocity v hits and sticks to another mass 2m at rest? We watch this collision from a car moving with velocity minus v over 2. In every case we find that the mass of the first object times its velocity, plus the mass of the second object times its velocity, is equal to the total mass of the final object times its velocity. These are all examples of the conservation of momentum. Starting from simple symmetrical cases we have demonstrated the law for more complex cases. We could in fact do it for any rational mass ratio, and since every ratio is exceedingly close to a rational ratio, we can handle every ratio as precisely as we wish.
